newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia again seeks investor in largest silver mine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia again seeks investor in largest silver mine.

text.p: Work at the country's largest silver mine in Russia's Far East has all but stopped, electricity has been shut off, and most workers are on forced holiday, waiting for an investor to come to their rescue.

In the earth at the Dukat mine are reserves of 14,000 tonnes of silver and 30 tonnes of gold, according to officials in the regional capital Magadan, an eight-hour flight east of Moscow. Yet not even two thirds of Russia's unmined silver has been enough to attract a suitor.
In two failed investment tender efforts this year, the Russian authorities have found no company willing to sink money into the mine because of a back debt estimated at between $50 and $80 million.

"In all the previous tenders they had barely enough participants because, while the deposit is very attractive, the debt is very ugly, and no one wants to assume that debt right now," said Sergei Kabyakov, a project specialist for Canada's Pan American Silver Corp.
Pan American has already bid twice on the ailing Dukat complex for a 49 percent stake, and remains interested in the mine, Kabyakov said. Workers own most of the rest of the shares.

In the first tender in January, the local authorities said they did not recognise the $168 million offer because there were no proper competitors. In the second try in April Pan American won the bid, pledging $36 million less for repairing the old plant, but pulled out after seeing the fine print.
"It was a case of misunderstanding," Kabyakov said. "They don't put everything into the statement."
THIRD TENDER IN A YEAR COMING SOON
Last month regional officials submitted to Moscow new guidelines for a new commercial tender they hope will finally bring an end to Dukat's misery.
They say they need to move quickly on the sale as the debt is growing daily and the entire region of about 7,500 people 600 km (370 miles) north of Magadan is dependent on the mine.

"We sent in the documents three weeks ago and we are tired of waiting," said Vecheslav Kobets, the Magadan region's deputy governor. "It is still not clear when the investment competition will take place."

But Igor Lipkin, chairman of the Russian Federal Property Fund, told Reuters he had not even received the latest proposals on Dukat, suggesting further delays as documents travel through the notorious labyrinth of Russia's bureaucracy.
"I still haven't seen the latest proposal," Lipkin said. "I'll have to call to get another copy."
Under draft rules local Property Fund officials sent to Moscow, the new bidding will start at 2.8 billion roubles ($482,000) for 139,584 shares, or 49 percent of the company.
The winner would be obliged to pay back wages and federal debt within a month, pay off $10 million in other debts within six months, and other debts over three years.

"Naturally, we had to change the conditions of the sale," said Olga Molchanova, deputy director of Magadan region's Property Fund. "It's not easy to find a firm ready to spend $75 million just to pay old debt; it's like throwing money into the wind."
Much of the debt was associated with the end of transport and other subsidies after the collapse of communism in 1991, officials say.
The new deal will not retain obligations to keep all 1,200 Dukat workers, and invest $77.7 million in refurbishing the ageing mine and related facilities as it did in April.
But regional officials and outside businesses said the complex needs $100-170 million in renovations in any case.

Alexander Fesik, the regional governor's spokesman, estimated that with proper investment the mine's output would reach 500 to 600 tonnes of silver a year -- worth $70 to $84 million at the current price.
But according to the regional government's industry department, the 15-year average annual output between 1980 and 1995 was 150 tonnes of silver, and fell to less than 50 tonnes last year.
SPECTRE OF BANKRUPTCY
Looming above the struggling enterprise is the spectre of bankruptcy, a mechanism much feared and rarely used in Russia although available for several years.

"I think the enterprise should have been declared bankrupt and sold to investors," Molchanova said. "Of course many creditors would suffer but then the enterprise would live again, taxes would get paid, and workers would keep their jobs."
Kabyakov said that under Russian law the licence to mine Dukat would revert back to the government after bankruptcy, giving the investor a heap of worthless old equipment.
But Kobets says bankruptcy will be the only option if the government fails to sell the minority share in the coming months.
"If we don't succeed on the next tender we will declare bankruptcy," he said. "The company could be profitable if the debts were taken care of. It would take a year to put in order."
